terms.definition: Wordplay on credo (I believe) and cor-dare (to give one's heart): to believe is to hand over the heart, entrusting oneself, not merely assenting to facts.
terms.nuance: For Ratzinger believing is entrusting, not program: faith belongs to "stand-understand", not "know-make"; the heart is given to a ground one did not make.

terms.definition: Distinguishes faith's content, fides quae (what is believed), from fides qua: the personal act of believing, the faith by which one believes.
terms.nuance: Ratzinger reverses the felt priority: by origin faith is "not a recitation of doctrines" but "conversion, an about-turn, a shift of being"; content lives in the act.

terms.definition: Belief without the name faith: the unavoidable basic decision every person makes about meaning; no one stands outside some act of entrusting.
terms.nuance: Ratzinger rules out unbelief in principle: positivist and Marxist alike stake life on meaning, for man "is bound to have some kind of “belief”"; credo is conversion, not acquisition.

terms.definition: Faith's central formula: not assent to something but trust in the You who upholds me, the personal character of Christian belief.
terms.nuance: The book's culmination: "its central formula is not “I believe in something”"; the meaning of the world is a person, and faith is "the encounter with the man Jesus".

terms.definition: The root shared by Amen and belief: truth, firm ground, loyalty, trust; faith as taking a stand on what upholds.
terms.nuance: Ratzinger rings the whole Creed with it: "In the harmony of “Credo” and “Amen”" the meaning becomes visible; believing is trustful standing toward logos, not blind surrender.

terms.definition: Even if God did not exist: conducting public life as though God were irrelevant, faith kept private, with nothing left for God to do.
terms.nuance: The 1989 preface's diagnosis: Christianity lived this way by default, and the bill arrives when "God is dead" is taken to heart and man becomes raw material.

terms.definition: God's answer to Moses at the burning bush: "I AM WHO I AM" (or: I am what I am), unfolded into the revealed name Yahweh.
terms.nuance: Ratzinger hears "a refusal to give a name" as much as a name: the answer cancels the name into mystery yet promises presence, identity as being-for.

terms.definition: Israel's revealed name of God, explained by I am; Ratzinger reads its root as being: the one who simply is, enduring presence and promise.
terms.nuance: He weds the Name to philosophical Being yet transforms both: "he is there for us", "he is our God"; being turns out to be faithful presence.

terms.definition: The patriarchal names for God: El, the personal highest God met on the I-You plane; Elohim, a plural form used for Israel's one God.
terms.nuance: Ratzinger reads the strange plural as a pointer past our categories: God "lies beyond them"; even the number one cannot contain him, a hint of Trinity.

terms.definition: God as the patriarchs met him: personal, promise-bound, tied to no shrine, the numen personale over against the local numen.
terms.nuance: The inner assumption of Yahweh-faith: relation before place, hope before power, for "He is not the god of a place but the god of men".

terms.definition: Not a definition of God's essence but his self-giving: to name himself is to become invocable, entering relation and coexistence with us.
terms.nuance: Ratzinger contrasts name with concept: concepts grasp things in themselves, but God's self-naming is "making himself nameable", "handing himself over to men", fulfilled when the name becomes a person.

terms.definition: The hidden God and the revealed God: biblical self-disclosure conceals as it reveals; the name withdraws into mystery while promising presence.
terms.nuance: In the burning bush both hold at once: "concealment and revelation" are simultaneous; the Name dissolves into mystery yet becomes invocable nearness.

terms.definition: The analogy of being: creatures resemble God only under a still greater unlikeness; all God-talk is analogical, never literal or exhaustive.
terms.nuance: Ratzinger invokes the Lateran rule whenever God is named: what we say is always outstripped, the difference remaining "greater than what they have in common".

terms.definition: True because made: "all that we can truly know is what we have made ourselves" (Vico); modernity adds the faciendum, the makeable future we must produce.
terms.nuance: Ratzinger diagnoses modernity's makability and Marxism's faciendum politics: belief cannot be consigned to fact or project, for meaning is received, never manufactured.

terms.definition: Word, reason, meaning: the mind at the heart of being, and John's title for Christ, in whom meaning is personal and has a face.
terms.nuance: Ratzinger makes logos faith's ground: meaning is received, not made, and is truth; "The indivisibility of meaning, ground, and truth" unites Creed and philosophy.

terms.definition: Myth, sacred story: the religious worldview the early Church refused when it chose truth over custom and the philosophers' God over the gods.
terms.nuance: He names the choice "opting for the logos as against any kind of myth", a definitive demythologization, and warns that retreat into piety repeats antiquity's failure.

terms.definition: Creation out of nothing: the world is sheer gift, matter included, held in being by a freedom that owes it nothing.
terms.nuance: It is the grammar of grace: the Virgin Birth replays creation, the God "who created being out of nothing", so salvation is new creation, never achievement.

terms.definition: Greek: of one substance with the Father. Nicaea's formula that the Son shares the Father's very being, "the standard of orthodoxy" from the fourth century.
terms.nuance: Ratzinger reads the formula as "a frontier notice": it "had been condemned in the third century" itself, usable only as baffled speech guarding the mystery.

terms.definition: Being and person: the Creed's one being in three Persons, oneness on the level of substance, threeness as relation.
terms.nuance: He revolutionizes the pair with Augustine: "accidents, only substance and relation"; person is pure relatedness, so relation is as primordial as substance.

terms.definition: Lord: the Greek Bible's substitute for the unspeakable divine Name, confessed of Jesus in the Creed as our Lord, the title the Cross redefines.
terms.nuance: Ratzinger redefines the title through the Cross: true lordship is pure self-giving; the cosmos bows before "the slaughtered Lamb", not before power.

terms.definition: Self-emptying: Christ's surrender of existence for himself to become servant, the Latin exinanivit, "he “emptied” himself", the hinge of the Philippians hymn.
terms.nuance: Ratzinger makes kenosis the key to divinity: "the pure movement of the “for”" is precisely his glory; the emptied one becomes lord of the whole cosmos.

terms.definition: For us: Christ's being is wholly directed to others, "the “for us”" around which the Bible gathers election, representation, and redemption.
terms.nuance: With Barth, Ratzinger calls this functional Christology: "the whole being of Jesus is a function" of "the “for us”"; there is no private “I” behind his work.

terms.definition: The last Adam: Christ as exemplary and final man who gathers humanity and carries it, with God, into its future.
terms.nuance: Ratzinger: "the exemplary man" oversteps humanity by pure openness, "final man, who takes man into his future"; his existence concerns all mankind, not one exception.

terms.definition: Christ's entry into death itself: the final loneliness and godforsakenness from which no voice returns, not a geography of torment beneath the earth.
terms.nuance: Ratzinger calls it the most modern article: solidarity, not scenery, for he passed "gate of our final loneliness" and "the abyss of our abandonment".

terms.definition: The last thing: history's end and goal, Christ's return, the world's omega and judgment, already breaking through in Jesus' Resurrection.
terms.nuance: Ratzinger collapses the distance: "end-eschatology" and Resurrection "are in reality one and the same thing"; the end has begun, "the eschatological happening".

terms.definition: Presence, coming: Christ's return in glory and the world's consummation, cried for in the early Church's Maran atha, "Our Lord, come".
terms.nuance: Ratzinger sets Maran atha against Dies irae: the first Christians waited with hope, not dread; the Creed's bare judgment-line must be read back within mercy.

terms.definition: The coming judge of living and dead: the last court of appeal that preserves justice in order to perfect love rather than destroy it.
terms.nuance: Ratzinger turns terror into hope: judgment is handed to our brother, "It is not a stranger who judges us"; the judge has suffered and knows us from within.

terms.definition: Effective sign of God's gift, baptism, Eucharist, penance, through which the Church is made one and grace becomes touchable.
terms.nuance: Constitutive, not ornamental: "Church and sacrament stand or fall together", and the Creed itself is baptismal, born in the sacrament of conversion.

terms.definition: According to the whole: the Church's wholeness, locally one around the bishop, universally one across all places and peoples.
terms.nuance: Not a boast but a demand: catholicity is "visible unity" of Word and sacrament, "the necessity for the unity of all the bishops with one another".

terms.definition: The fellowship formed by the holy gifts, Eucharist, baptism, forgiveness, binding the baptized across the earth and beyond death.
terms.nuance: Ratzinger recovers the sacramental root: sanctorum "does not refer to persons but means the holy gifts"; communion is made by worship, not mustered by holy people.

terms.definition: The promise that the whole embodied person, not a separated soul, lives on, awakened by God at the end, together with all mankind.
terms.nuance: Ratzinger defuses the scandal: the hope concerns "the one, undivided man", not reassembled bodies; "man can no longer totally perish" because God loves him into life.
